problems: Minor: the page is sound. The only nuance worth noting is that the UA-default focus outline (tabOrder shows outlineColor rgb(0,95,204)) provides a focus-state cue on the link, but F73 explicitly requires a resting-state non-color distinction and its note states a cue available only on hover/focus still fails — so this does not undermine the 'failed' verdict.
None material. The failure is genuine and the outcome label (failed) is correct.

Minor framing nuance: F73 classifies lightness as 'not color', so a same-hue pair at >=3:1 lightness would PASS 1.4.1. The page correctly lands BELOW that (2.04:1), so it genuinely fails - but the .md/CSS comment phrasing ('color (hue) alone') is slightly loose since the technical cue here is a lightness step, not hue. The outcome is unaffected.

DETECTABILITY UNDERCUT: The case authors link-vs-body lightness contrast at 2.30:1 (verified: link #1f6f43 vs body #2b2b2b = 2.30:1, below F73's 3:1 escape-hatch). axe-core's automated link-in-text-block rule evaluates the RESTING computed style and would flag a sub-3:1 link with no resting non-color cue (computed text-decoration:none, font-weight:400 confirmed). The page's stated human-judgment rationale (compare rest-vs-hover; apply F73 'hover-only still fails') is moot for automation because axe never consults :hover and fails on resting contrast alone -> requiresHumanJudgment is effectively false for this corpus.

DOC IMPRECISION (not outcome-changing): The .md doc and the HTML comment claim 'No :focus rule, so keyboard users also get colour-only at rest.' Dynamic check with mouse parked at 0,0 then Tab shows the keyboard-focused link gets the UA default focus ring (outline: auto 1px) although it correctly gets NO CSS underline. So a keyboard user traversing links DOES receive a non-color cue on the focused link. This does not rescue the F73 failure (focus ring helps neither scanning/reading, grayscale, nor touch users) so outcome stays 'failed', but the keyboard claim is overstated.

OUTCOME CONTRADICTED BY THE CITED TECHNIQUE ITSELF: F73 (wcag-techniques/failures/F73.html line 10) states verbatim 'If the link is a different color and bold it would not fail because the boldness is not color dependent.' F73's test procedure (line 44) explicitly lists 'bolded' as a valid non-color distinguishing means. The links here are font-weight:700 in their RESTING state (case-05.html line 28: '.course a { color:#9d1b3d; font-weight:700; text-decoration:none }'), confirmed by computed style fontWeight:'700'. So F73 check #1 is TRUE for every link -> the failure condition does NOT apply -> the page PASSES F73, it does not fail. Claimed outcome 'failed' is wrong.

MECHANISM IS NOT A 1.4.1 MECHANISM: The doc's real argument is that bold is 'shared with <strong>' so it can't distinguish links from non-link emphasis. But 1.4.1/F73 requires that a link be distinguishable from SURROUNDING BODY TEXT without color, not that the cue be unique vs other emphasized text. Body prose is normal weight (#222, 400); links are bold (700). The bold cue survives grayscale, so a color-blind/grayscale user DOES perceive links as distinct from body prose. The doc's claim that grayscale users 'see only undifferentiated bold prose' is false for the link-vs-body comparison.

SELF-REFUTING DOC: the 'Why automated tools miss it' section (case-05.md lines 43-49) admits a scanner 'would, if anything, judge that sufficient' because 'links are bold and colored' -- which is exactly F73's own conclusion. The doc invents a stricter rule (cue must be unique vs emphasis) that F73 does not contain.

SIBLING MISFIT: case-01/02/03/04/06 keep links at normal weight (color is the sole resting cue) -> genuine F73 failures; case-04 uses bold only on :focus-visible (correctly failing per F73's hover/focus note). case-05 is the only case giving links PERSISTENT resting bold, which F73 says passes. It is structurally inconsistent with its own failure family.

Citation text itself is verbatim and from the correct document (F73 line 5) -- the defect is not a fabricated quote but a misapplication: the quote describes 'removing the underline and leaving only color', whereas this page leaves color AND bold, which the same document explicitly exempts on line 10.

Minor framing nuance (not a label defect): the .md says the hover/focus underline is merely 'supplementary' and '3:1 lightness is what carries conformance'. That is correct for the 1.4.1 OUTCOME, but G183's formal Expected Results require BOTH check #1 (3:1 luminance) AND check #2 (hover enhancement), and G183 explicitly states 'Hover or focus style changes alone are not sufficient.' The page does provide the hover/focus underline (CSS line 33), so it satisfies the full G183 procedure regardless; the passed label is unaffected.

The .md's 'failure-mechanism: NONE' and the term 'errorIsReal' are semantically inverted for a TRUE-NEGATIVE control: there is intentionally no accessibility error here. The page correctly represents a PASS scenario, so the documented outcome (passed) is real/correct — but reviewers should note errorIsReal=true here means 'the documented PASS scenario is genuine', not 'an accessibility defect exists'.

Minor doc-vs-code wording inconsistency (no functional impact): case-07.md line 24 describes the rule as color:inherit while the actual CSS (case-07.html line 31) uses literal color:#202124; equivalent because body is #202124, but prose should match code.
No accessibility issue exists by design (TRUE-NEGATIVE/inapplicable) — this is intended, not a defect.

Minor prose inaccuracy: doc/HTML comment claim red-on-white contrast is 5.9:1; computed value is 5.62:1 (#c62828 lum 0.1368 vs white). Does not affect the SC verdict (still >4.5:1) but is a numeric error that should be corrected.

Edge case worth flagging (does NOT overturn 'failed'): the required-label red (#c62828) vs optional-label black (#1a1a1a) computes to 3.10:1 luminosity contrast — marginally above F81's note threshold of 3:1 that can rescue a color-only distinction by 'lightness'. The case still genuinely fails because (a) 3.10:1 is borderline-perceptible at best and (b) even a greyscale/colorblind viewer who notices two grey shades cannot determine WHICH shade means 'required' — the sole legend ('Required fields appear in red') is itself color-keyed and never resolves the mapping. The borderline luminosity actually reinforces that a naive automated luminosity check could mis-pass it, so human judgment is required.

Minor nuance (not a defect): the required field's left border differs in WIDTH too (3px vs 1px), so it is not STRICTLY a pure-color difference. However this 2px delta on one edge is not a recognizable 'required' indicator on its own — there is no legend/text/instruction explaining it, and the salient, designer-intended cue is the red hue. The page still fails 1.4.1 because there is no ADEQUATE non-color alternative; the doc could be slightly more precise by acknowledging the width delta and arguing it is not perceivable/meaningful as a non-color cue.

The .md also asserts the page 'would also fail 1.3.1/3.3.2 programmatically' — true and a checker could catch the missing required/aria-required there, but that is a DIFFERENT SC; for 1.4.1's visible-non-color-alternative requirement no automated tool flags it, so the human-judgment claim for THIS SC holds.

DOC FACTUAL ERROR (does not change outcome): The .md 'Exact accessibility mechanism' section claims the ::before bullet is 'invisible to AT entirely' and the screen reader hears 'Patient full name' with 'no bullet'. The Chromium AX tree REFUTES this: required textboxes are named '•Patient full name', '•Insurance member ID', '•Contact name', '•Contact phone' (the ::before bullet IS folded into the accessible name; optional fields get clean names). The HTML comment lines 24/42-43 making the same 'invisible to the accessibility tree' claim are likewise inaccurate in Chromium.

The doc's AT-invisibility claim is a secondary (1.3.1/4.1.2-flavored) embellishment that is false; the genuine 1.4.1 failure rests on the sighted color-blind user's perception, not on the screen-reader path, so the verdict is unaffected — but the inaccurate sentence should ideally be corrected or removed.

None material. This is an intentional TRUE-NEGATIVE (a PASS case), so by design there is no accessibility issue on the page — errorIsReal=false is the correct/expected state here, not a defect. The documented 'passed' outcome is correct.
Minor stylistic note only (not a defect): the .md cites TWO references (G205 + use-of-color Understanding); the prompt's 'named' citation is the second one. Both are accurate.
No defect: this is an intentional TRUE-NEGATIVE that correctly PASSES 1.4.1 via the lightness escape hatch. errorIsReal=false is the designed state, not a flaw.

Minor design note (not a defect): the legend paragraph (line 65-66) textually states 'Required field labels are a lighter green; optional field labels are dark charcoal. The two are also clearly different in shade' — this is an extra textual description of the color convention. It does not annotate which individual fields are required, so users still rely on the visual color/lightness per field; the lightness-escape-hatch reasoning remains the operative pass mechanism. Worth noting only because it slightly softens the 'purely color' boundary purity.

Doc narrative inaccuracy (not a page defect): the .md and prompt say 'Seven visually identical bold labels differ only in hue for the two errored ones', but the form has exactly FIVE labeled required fields (first, last, dob, carrier, member), two of which error. The count 'seven' is wrong.
Doc L* figures are slightly off (says red L*~39 / ink L*~22; actual ~41.1 / ~17.0) — directionally fine and does not change the verdict.

Required-ness is encoded via a custom data-req attribute rather than the HTML required attribute (required=false on every field at runtime). This is intentional/realistic and strengthens the 'automated tools miss it' claim, but worth noting that the page therefore also has no programmatic required semantics.

Minor doc imprecision (not a defect): the .md says every summary row has 'the same weight and size' with nothing else marking failures, but the .errsum card also has a red border-left:4px accent (style line 32). This is a card-level accent, not a per-item cue, so it does NOT identify WHICH three rows failed and does not weaken the F81 failure — worth noting only for precision.

Borderline-but-defensible mechanism nuance: on mismatch the box-shadow appears (presence vs absence), which a pedant could argue is a non-color change independent of hue. The case survives because the 2px shadow's MEANING (error) is carried by hue alone and is visually confusable with ordinary focus/elevation styling (the :focus state also uses a 2px outline). This is exactly the human-judgment borderline 1.4.1 review exists for, but reviewers should be aware the failure rests on 'hue is the only meaningful differentiator,' not 'no visual change at all.'

The .md doc's accessibility-mechanism section briefly mixes in 3.3.1/4.1.3 concerns (no aria-invalid / silent class toggle). These are correctly scoped OUT of the 1.4.1 verdict in the doc ('1.4.1's specific failure is the absence of a VISIBLE non-color cue'), but the overlap could invite confusion about which SC is under test.

Minor: the failing #children field is also the only EMPTY field (value="") while the valid fields are pre-filled (adults=2, income=2840). An empty number field is not itself an error cue (empty is a normal state), so the verdict stands, but the page would be a cleaner isolation of the color-only mechanism if all fields were filled and only the border color differed. Not a defect that changes the outcome.

Minor authoring nit (not a WCAG defect): the generic role=alert banner (line 68) and aria-invalid together are exactly the 3.3.1/4.1.2/4.1.3 channels the doc says do NOT discharge 1.4.1 — this is intentional and correctly described, but reviewers should note the page would also have a separate (out-of-scope here) 3.3.1 'error not specifically identified' concern; it does not affect the 1.4.1 label.

Minor citation-vs-page mismatch (not outcome-affecting): the prompt/.md leans on G205, whose second sentence (verified verbatim, G205.html line 21) requires the text cue be part of the programmatically determinable NAME of the control. On this page the error text is in the field's DESCRIPTION (aria-describedby='name-err'), not its name (AX name is just 'Name on card'). The pass is really carried by G14 (info also in text) + the visible icon shape, not strict G205. The 'passed' label is still correct because 1.4.1 only requires a non-color VISIBLE means, which the text+triangle satisfy.

As the .md candidly states, automated tools also pass this page; its value as a corpus item is purely as a true-negative boundary case for human judgment, not as a defect an automated checker would otherwise miss.

No defects affecting the 1.4.1 verdict. (Out-of-scope, correctly noted in the doc: the invalid #amount has no aria-invalid and no per-field error text/programmatic association, which are genuine 3.3.1/4.1.2 gaps — but those are different SCs and do not affect the 1.4.1 'passed' label.)

Minor scope note (not a defect): F13 is officially a failure of BOTH SC 1.1.1 and 1.4.1 (per F13.html title line 4/8), and the omitted resolved fact is arguably read even more directly as a 1.1.1 text-alternative failure. Filing it under 1.4.1 is still correct because the membership distinction is encoded purely as a color difference (red vs green bars) with no non-color visible alternative; the .md itself acknowledges the dual mapping, so this is a legitimately dual-mapped technique, not a misclassification.

Minor residual ambiguity: the figcaption lists the five programs and five amounts in the same descending order, so a diligent reader COULD infer positional pairing (Direct food aid = $1.08M = largest) and thus reverse-engineer that teal = Direct food aid. The phrasing 'which together received' (aggregate, no 'respectively') is deliberately non-binding, so this remains an inference rather than text-available information — F13 is still satisfied (image conveys the binding via color; aria-label does not). This is the only point a skeptical reviewer could push on, and it does not overturn the failed verdict.

Minor (not a defect, but worth noting for any future substring-based scorer): the aria-describedby description DOES contain the literal strings 'Verde' and 'Calloway' (line 78), listed as the five-county ROSTER, not as the warned set. A naive name-presence checker could false-pass. The page is still correctly labeled failed because the warned-membership BINDING ({Verde, Calloway} = under Severe Heat Warning) is conveyed only by the red polygon fill (#c62f25) and never asserted in text; the prose explicitly defers to the map ('shaded red on the map'). This actually strengthens the requiresHumanJudgment claim.

The same long-description text is also a visible

below the image, so it is not screen-reader-only; but since that prose also omits the binding, the F13 failure holds for all users who cannot perceive the red fill (blind, low-vision, protanopia, greyscale/e-ink).

Minor framing overreach (does not invalidate the case): the .md/HTML lean heavily on color-vision-deficiency ('two lines of nearly indistinguishable hue', 'near-identical hues'). The actual strokes are #1f9d55 green and #d8392b red, which differ substantially in LUMINANCE, so a deuteranope/protanope could likely still tell the two lines apart by lightness. The real, robust failure is the non-visual one (the aria-label/text alternative omits the color-encoded comparison entirely), which F13 covers regardless of CVD distinguishability. The CVD argument is the weakest pillar; the case stands on the text-alternative-omission pillar.

The 'temporal/comparative twist' is genuine but note the headline 'We turned the corner this spring' DOES narratively assert a turnaround in text; what is missing is the specific per-month profit/loss/crossover (which months were losses, when the lines cross). The failure is correctly the missing per-month comparison, not a total absence of any narrative — the doc's wording ('never resolves the profit/loss story') is fair but slightly overstated given that prose.

SELF-DEFEATING MECHANISM: The long description (#boardDesc, lines 80-87) lists every service WITH ITS METRIC. The two RED/down tiles carry unmistakable failure-WORD metrics in text: 'auth-gateway (timeout)' and 'payments-worker (no heartbeat)', while the six GREEN services carry benign latency readings ('p95 142ms', 'p95 98ms', etc.). Decoded SVG (lines 74-77) confirms: red fill #c22b27 on exactly auth-gateway/'timeout' and payments-worker/'no heartbeat'; green fill #1f7a3d on the other six. Thus the down-state IS conveyed in a non-color text channel and is bound to the service names in prose.

OUTCOME LABEL WRONG: Combined with 'Two of the eight services are currently down' (line 86) and exactly two failure-word metrics (timeout, no heartbeat), a screen-reader or color-blind user can reliably identify the two down services from prose alone, with no reliance on red/green. Under the cited Test 13.A this is the required 'another visual, onscreen method ... which does not use color' — i.e. arguably a PASS, not a clean 'failed'. The claimed F13 mechanism (color is the ONLY channel for which-are-down) is false for this page.

DOC OVERSTATEMENT: The .md (lines 11-12, 46-48) and the HTML author comment (lines 21-25) assert the prose 'never NAMES which two' / 'never resolves it', treating count-without-identities as 'textbook F13'. But F13's canonical case fails because the text gives NO non-color cue to the identities; here the metric words ('timeout','no heartbeat') functionally resolve the identities. The page contradicts its own intended mechanism.

Minor secondary signal: aria-describedby #boardDesc lives inside a collapsed <details> and Chromium AX resolved description=None at load (inspect.js axTree), but textContent is still associable; this does not rescue the case since even when read the prose self-resolves the down identities.
No defects found. This is a deliberate TRUE NEGATIVE / PASS boundary case, and it is correctly constructed: there is no accessibility issue and none is claimed.

Minor: the document's `errorIsReal` framing — for a PASS case the relevant question is whether the documented PASS phenomenon is genuine, which it is. No barrier exists for any user (AT, colour-blind, monochrome).

Minor (non-disqualifying): line 38 has invalid SVG attribute height="auto" which throws a benign console error 'Expected length, "auto"'. The map still renders (width=100% applies; inspect box w=696, h=0 for the zero-height polyline is expected geometry), so it does not affect the 1.4.1 mechanism or page integrity, but it is sloppy markup that should be cleaned up (e.g. drop height or use a viewBox-derived value).

Minor confound (not disqualifying): the .pipeline container is role="img" with an aria-label that lists the six stage names but omits pass/fail status, and the matched .stage.fail is role="none" in the AX tree. This means a screen-reader user ALSO loses the status (a layered 1.1.1-style barrier). It does not contradict the 1.4.1 visual failure since the aria-label is not an onscreen non-color cue, but the case is not a perfectly 'clean' 1.4.1-only isolation — the status is doubly inaccessible.

Citation formatting: the doc quotes 'An error indicator cannot use color alone as an indicator.' while the source file (refs/trusted-tester/sc-1.4.1-use-of-color.md line 27) has inline bold markup 'An **error indicator cannot use color alone** as an indicator.' This is a markdown-formatting difference only (text identical) — acceptable, noted for completeness.

Minor: the prompt's restatement of the citation reads 'based strong on the colors' (an artifact of stripping the <strong> tag); the actual .md doc quotes it correctly as 'based both on the colors used', which is verbatim from use-of-color.html line 141 where 'both' is wrapped in <strong>. No defect in the page/doc — only in the prompt paraphrase.

Minor robustness note: the failure mechanism is strongest via CVD (red #d64545 oxygen vs dark #333740 carbon). The grayscale-collapse argument is secondary/weaker (the three fills actually have fairly distinct luminance: ~#333740 dark, ~#d64545 mid, ~#eef1f4 near-white), but the core 1.4.1 principle (per-atom element identity conveyed by color alone with no symbol/number fallback) holds regardless.
No defect found — correctly-labelled true negative.

Minor: both buttons are type=submit inside <form onsubmit="return false;">, so the red 'cancel' button does not functionally cancel anything (it submits and is no-op'd). This is acceptable for a static perceivability fixture but means the page demonstrates only the visual/AX encoding, not live action behavior.

Cosmetic: the doc/selector uses form.actions to mean a container, but class="actions" is on the <form> itself; form.actions button.btn--proceed still resolves correctly as a descendant selector, so no real defect — just slightly non-obvious naming.

None that undermine the case. The .md claims 'identical underline' but the CSS never explicitly sets text-decoration (only a:hover{text-decoration:none}); links rely on the browser-default underline, which is identical for both classes anyway, so the distinction is still color-only and the claim holds in substance.

Minor wording nuance: the AX name 'Order a marriage certificate online (VitalChek)' contains a parenthetical, but it names a service, not the new-window action, so it does not provide a non-color cue — claim unaffected.

Minor (not a defect): the color legend swatches at lines 52-54 use inline style= attributes, which the V3_HTML_NOSTYLE ablation strips from HTML evidence; the legend's color-to-track-name binding is inherently visual regardless, so this does not affect case validity but is worth noting for the evidence-lane ablation.

Minor doc imprecision (not a defect in the mechanism): the in-page header legend 'Toggles in green are on; grey are off' (html:56) is itself color-dependent — it tells the user what the colors mean but, because all four toggles are visually identical to a grayscale/color-deficient user, it does not let them determine any individual switch's state. It does not rescue the page from 1.4.1, but the doc never mentions this legend exists, so a reviewer could mistakenly think a text cue is present.

Minor SC-attribution imprecision in the .md/HTML comment: it says 'each pill colour also passes 1.4.3 against the page background.' The pills are non-text UI components, so their boundary contrast is governed by 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast), not 1.4.3. Computed pill-vs-bg is ~2.7:1 (below 3:1), so that claim is doubly off — wrong SC and the value would actually fail 1.4.11. This is orthogonal to the 1.4.1 verdict but is an inaccurate rationale.

Citation in case-06.md is a compressed paraphrase rather than a verbatim quote (it stitches the two G14 sentences and normalizes spelling); the underlying G14.html does contain the example verbatim and supports the claim, so this is minor.
This is an intentional TRUE NEGATIVE/passing boundary case: errorIsReal=false by design; the validated claim is the 'passed' outcome, which reasoning + AX tree confirm is correct.
None material. This is an intentional TRUE NEGATIVE (passing) case, so there is no accessibility issue to confirm — by design. errorIsReal=false reflects that absence, not a defect.

Minor citation framing nit (not a defect): the .md labels the source 'Understanding 1.4.1 / G14.html', but G14 is a WCAG Technique (wcag-techniques/general/G14.html), not part of the Understanding doc. The technique ID, file, and quoted sentence are all correct, so the claim is fully supported.

Minor (non-blocking): the page satisfies 1.4.1 via TWO independent non-color cues — the lightness escape hatch AND the leading +/- signs (present in DOM and AX tree as '+$2,410.00' / '-$6.75'). The doc states the escape hatch alone governs the verdict, which is correct, but the +/- signs mean the PASS is over-determined rather than a pure isolated escape-hatch test. Verdict is unaffected.

Borderline-by-design (intentional, not a defect): inter-element contrast is 3.155:1, only 0.155 above the 3:1 floor; this is what makes it a meaningful test, but any rounding or color drift would flip the verdict.

Doc/HTML comment claim 'no word mild/spicy ... no per-dish text label' is slightly imprecise: one mild dish's description reads 'Mixed vegetables, coconut, green chilli (mild)' (line 64) — an incidental textual cue for that single dish. It does not rescue the page (all three hot dishes and the rest carry no spice word; the AX tree exposes only plain StaticText dish names with zero spice semantics), so the verdict stands, but the absolute 'no per-dish text label' wording is inaccurate.

Minor numeric drift in the stated contrast ratios: doc says mild/bg ~5.1:1 and hot/bg ~5.4:1, but computed sRGB values are 4.80:1 and 5.09:1 respectively. Both still pass 1.4.3 (>=4.5:1 for normal text) so the 'pure use-of-colour, not contrast' framing holds; only the rounded figures are ~0.3 high.

Second citation (wcag-understanding/use-of-color.html intent-note negation) could not be file-verified — no refs/wcag-understanding/use-of-color.html exists locally. It is a paraphrased/negation gloss rather than a verbatim quote and is not the named primary citation, so low risk, but it is unverifiable in-repo.

Minor (not disqualifying): the inputs carry pre-filled values (malformed email 'priya.raman@@example', empty 'years', empty 'cover' textarea), so a fully-sighted non-colorblind reviewer could partly infer validity from field CONTENT rather than color. However the page frames validity as a server/client review result ('We checked your details'), and valid empty-looking fields exist too, so color remains the only DESIGNATED carrier of the accepted/needs-attention status — the 1.4.1 failure stands.

This is an inapplicable/non-failure (escape-hatch) case, so there is no positive accessibility defect to confirm: errorIsReal=false because no use-of-color failure exists on the page (the doc's whole claim is that 1.4.1 does NOT apply). expectedOutcomeCorrect=true because the documented 'inapplicable' label is correct and well-supported. Reviewers comparing to failure cases should not read errorIsReal=false here as a defect in the page.

Minor scoping nuance (not a defect): the page intentionally co-locates a real but DIFFERENT-criterion problem (poor link discoverability -> 1.3.1/2.4.4). The doc correctly flags this, but a careless labeler could mistake the page for a failure of those other SCs. The 1.4.1 verdict itself is sound.
No defects found. This is a correctly-constructed PASS (non-failure / escape-hatch) case for SC 1.4.1.

Minor cosmetic note (not a defect): the .md doc rounds the background-relative contrasts to ~7.2:1 and ~7.9:1; recomputed values are 7.01:1 (unvisited) and 7.66:1 (visited). Both still comfortably exceed the 4.5:1 SC 1.4.3 minimum, so the conclusion is unaffected. The load-bearing inter-link ratio (1.09:1, <3:1) matches the doc exactly.

Minor (not a defect): the element-under-test selector `.pill input:checked + label` resolves to a node whose AX role is `LabelText` with an empty accessible name (the name flows to the associated radio). This is correct/expected for an `<input>+<label>` pair and does not affect the 1.4.1 verdict, but reviewers using the selector's ax.name as a sanity check should note it is intentionally empty.
